A person who checks their own work carefully, again and again, eventually stops needing to check it quite so carefully, which is the whole point.
There's real value in a tool that resists the temptation to always tell you good news, even when good news is more comfortable to hear.
The quiet discipline of tracking something honestly, day after unremarkable day, tends to matter far more in the long run than any single motivated burst of effort.
Attention to detail is rarely glamorous in the moment, but it's almost always the thing people point to later when explaining real mastery.
A fair measurement treats a bad day and a good day with the same honesty, which is exactly what makes it trustworthy over time.
Somewhere between hoping you're improving and actually knowing it, there's a habit of honest, unglamorous attention to your own real numbers, and that habit is the difference.
Fish and visitors stink after three days.
